William Tell. Gioachino Rossini's William Tell, composed in 1829, is a four-act French grand opera based on Friedrich Schiller's play Wilhelm Tell. Set in the Swiss Alps in the fourteenth century, it depicts the Swiss struggle for independence against the tyrannical occupying Austrian Habsburgs, led by the cruel governor Gessler. The legendary marksman William Tell emerges as the leader of the rebellion. After refusing to bow to Gessler's hat placed on a pole, Tell is arrested and forced to shoot an apple off his young son Jemmy's head with a crossbow. Tell succeeds, but reveals he had a second arrow intended for Gessler had he failed. Tell escapes, kills Gessler, and leads the Swiss to victory. This was Rossini's final opera, written when he was only thirty-seven, after which he retired from opera composition.

William Tell is the Swiss patriot and archer whose defiance of Austrian authority sparks the cantons to rise in rebellion. Gessler is the tyrannical Austrian governor of Schwyz and Uri who orders Tell's ordeal and represents imperial Habsburg oppression. Arnold Melchthal is a Swiss conspirator torn between his love for the Austrian princess Mathilde and his duty to his country, particularly after Gessler executes his elderly father. Jemmy is Tell's brave son who holds the apple on his head during the famous test of marksmanship. Mathilde is a Habsburg princess who opposes Gessler's cruelty, rescues Jemmy from execution, and ultimately sides with the Swiss patriots.

The William Tell Overture is one of the most famous pieces of classical music in the world, consisting of four movements: Dawn, Storm, Call to the Cows, and the iconic March of the Swiss Soldiers, featuring galloping brass. Sois immobile, Be still, is Tell's Act Three aria, sung to Jemmy before the apple shot, advising his son to pray, remain completely still, and keep his eyes on the ground. Asile hérédaire, Ancestral refuge, is Arnold's challenging Act Four tenor aria, lamenting his father's death and expressing his grief before leading the rebels.

Rossini was a dominant figure in early nineteenth-century opera. William Tell was a major influence on the French Grand Opera genre, contrasting sharply with his earlier comic masterpiece The Barber of Seville.
